in_text_mentions: At 15 days, he developed erythroderma and desquamation, initially treated with emollients without improvement. At 24 days, he presented with fever and was admitted to our department. On admission, he weighed 3850 g (150 g loss). Examination showed diffuse erythroderma, desquamation, alopecia, and absent eyelashes and eyebrows (Fig 1, A and B). Abdominal examination revealed a soft abdomen, a liver palpable 1 cm below the costal margin and a nonpalpable spleen.Fig 1A, Erythroderma associated with exfoliative dermatitis. B, Alopecia associated with generalized exfoliative dermatitis.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of an infant with diffuse scaling and erythema of the face and upper trunk, with sparse scalp hair. The article title and in-text mentions identify Omenn syndrome, a rare variant of SCID, and the caption/in-text support skin scaling, alopecia, and pustules. The image is a real patient clinical photo; no third-party copyright is indicated.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of an infant's back, neck and scalp showing a diffuse erythematous, scaly, hyperpigmented rash. The article title and in-text describe atypical Omenn syndrome due to ADA deficiency, and the caption/in-text explicitly link this diffuse rash (Figure 1) to the patient's immunodeficiency, supporting attribution to Omenn syndrome. Typicality is atypical per the article title ('Atypical Omenn Syndrome'). Age (2 months) and ethnicity (Somali) are stated in the text; skin tone is visibly dark. [raw subtype: atypical Omenn syndrome due to adenosine deaminase deficiency]
panels.attribution_text: Joshi et al. Atypical Omenn Syndrome due to Adenosine Deaminase Deficiency.. Case reports in immunology 2012. doi:10.1155/2012/919241. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Diffuse rash in an infant with ADA deficiency.
in_text_mentions: A 2-month-old Somali boy, born to consanguineous parents, presented to our hospital with concerns for immunodeficiency. The initial symptoms included cough, diffuse skin rash (Figure 1), hepatosplenomegaly, and a sepsis-like syndrome. A complete sepsis workup was negative, except for an absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) of 0, which triggered evaluation for an underlying primary immunodeficiency. T-, B- and NK-cell quantitation in blood revealed a T-B-NK- phenotype consistent with Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID).
